learn.hook: Helen Keller could not see or hear — yet she wrote books, travelled the world and earned a college degree!
points: Helen Keller (1880–1968) was an American writer. An illness took away her sight and hearing when she was about 19 months old.

Her teacher Anne Sullivan taught her words by spelling them into her hand. Her big breakthrough came when she understood that the letters spelled into her palm meant the 'water' pouring over her other hand.
In 1904 she graduated from Radcliffe College — the first deafblind person to earn a Bachelor of Arts degree.
'Three Days to See' is an essay in which she imagines what she would look at if she could see for three days.
An essay is a short piece of prose on one subject, giving the writer's thoughts and feelings.

example.q: Read this short piece in the spirit of the essay: "If I could see for just one day, I would first look at my mother's face. Then I would gaze at a marigold garland, bright orange and gold. At night I would lie on the roof and count the stars until I fell asleep." What is the writer asking us to value?
steps: List what the writer wants to see: a loved face, colours, the stars.
These are everyday sights we often ignore.
So the message is to notice and treasure what we can see.
example.answer: To treasure the ordinary sights around us — faces, colours and the night sky — instead of taking them for granted.

learn.reallife: Next time you see a sunset or your friend's smile, pause for a moment and really look — that is what Helen Keller asked people to do.

games.title: Helen Keller facts
items: She was born in Alabama, USA, in 1880.
Helen Keller could neither see nor hear.
An illness in early childhood took away both sight and hearing.
Anne Sullivan was Helen Keller's teacher.
'Three Days to See' is a poem.
It is an essay — a piece of prose.
Helen Keller never learned to read.
She read using Braille and wrote many books.

games.title: Helen Keller's life
items: She is born in Alabama, USA (1880).
An illness takes away her sight and hearing (1882).

quiz.q: How did Helen Keller lose her sight and hearing?
options: In a fall from a horse
In an accident when she was 20
After an illness when she was about 19 months old
quiz.explain: She became deaf and blind after an illness as a baby, at about 19 months.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a cause instead of recalling the fact

quiz.q: Who taught Helen Keller by spelling words into her hand?
quiz.explain: Anne Sullivan became Helen's teacher in 1887 and spelled words into her palm.
quiz.mistake: Picks another famous woman of the same time

quiz.q: 'Three Days to See' by Helen Keller is:
quiz.explain: It is written in prose and shares the writer's thoughts — an essay.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every famous piece of writing is a poem or story

quiz.q: What is an essay?
options: A list of words and their meanings
A story acted on a stage
A short piece of prose on one subject, giving the writer's ideas
quiz.explain: Essays are in prose (not verse) and share a writer's thoughts on one topic.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up essays with poems, plays or dictionaries

quiz.q: What is the main message of 'Three Days to See'?
options: People who cannot see cannot enjoy life
We should use our senses fully and not take them for granted
quiz.explain: Helen Keller urges sighted people to look closely at the world as if they might lose their sight tomorrow.
quiz.mistake: Picks an idea that is the opposite of her hopeful message

quiz.q: Helen Keller was the first deafblind person to earn:
quiz.explain: She graduated from Radcliffe College in 1904 with a BA degree.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a famous award

quiz.q: 'If I could see for just one day, I would first look at my mother's face.' What would the writer look at first?
quiz.explain: The word 'first' tells us the mother's face comes before the garland and the stars.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the order word 'first'

quiz.q: To 'take something for granted' means to:
options: not value it because you always have it
give it away as a gift
quiz.explain: When we take sight for granted, we forget how precious it is.
quiz.mistake: Reads the idiom word by word

teach.ask: Gappu heard about 'Three Days to See'. Who wrote it, and what is it about?
teach.praise: Wow! I'll look at the sky with fresh eyes today!
teach.nudge: And what does she want us to do with our senses?

learn.hook: Your nose can recognise the smell of hot jalebis even before you see the shop!
points: We have five senses: sight (eyes), hearing (ears), smell (nose), taste (tongue) and touch (skin).
Sensory words help readers imagine: glittering (sight), crackling (sound), fragrant (smell), tangy (taste), velvety (touch).
Braille is a reading system of raised dots invented by Louis Braille of France. Each Braille cell has six dot positions.
People who are deaf may use sign language; India has its own Indian Sign Language (ISL).
Melodious means sweet-sounding; fragrant means sweet-smelling.

example.q: Which senses are used in: 'The sizzling jalebis smelled sweet and felt sticky in my fingers'?

learn.reallife: Lifts, ATMs and some medicine boxes have Braille dots so that people who cannot see can use them.

quiz.q: Which word appeals to our sense of hearing?
quiz.explain: Rustling is the sound of dry leaves or paper moving.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up sound words with smell, touch or sight words

quiz.q: 'The mogra flowers were fragrant.' Which sense does 'fragrant' appeal to?
quiz.explain: Fragrant means having a sweet smell.
quiz.mistake: Thinks of how flowers look instead of the meaning of 'fragrant'

quiz.q: Who invented the Braille system of reading?
quiz.explain: Louis Braille of France created the raised-dot system that is named after him.
quiz.mistake: Picks another famous inventor

quiz.q: How many dot positions are there in one Braille cell?
quiz.explain: A Braille cell has 6 dot positions in two columns of three; different patterns stand for different letters.
quiz.mistake: Guesses without knowing the 2-by-3 pattern

quiz.q: Which word appeals to our sense of touch?
quiz.explain: Rough describes how something feels to our skin.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up touch with other senses

quiz.q: Which sense organ helps us taste food?
quiz.explain: Taste buds on the tongue tell sweet, sour, salty and bitter.
quiz.mistake: Confuses taste with smell, which also helps with flavour

quiz.q: What does 'melodious' mean?
quiz.explain: Melodious comes from 'melody' — a tune — so it means pleasant to hear.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the word to its root 'melody'

quiz.q: Which sentence uses the sense of taste?
quiz.explain: Sour is a taste.
quiz.mistake: Does not match the describing word to its sense

teach.ask: Gappu wonders why Helen Keller said we should treasure our senses. What are our senses and why should we value them?
teach.praise: Tweet! I can see, hear, smell, taste and touch — I'm so lucky!
teach.nudge: Name the senses, and tell me why they are precious.

learn.hook: Good, better, best! Some adjectives change completely when we compare.
points: Positive degree describes one thing: tall, beautiful.
Comparative degree compares two things and is often followed by 'than': taller, more beautiful.
Superlative degree compares three or more and usually takes 'the': the tallest, the most beautiful.
Long adjectives use more/most: more precious, most precious.
Irregular forms: good–better–best, bad–worse–worst, many–more–most, little–less–least. Spelling: big–bigger, happy–happier.

example.q: Complete: 'The Taj Mahal looks ___ (beautiful) at sunrise than at noon.'
steps: Two times are compared (sunrise and noon), and 'than' follows → comparative.
'Beautiful' is a long word, so we use 'more'.

learn.reallife: Shops say 'Bigger! Better! Best!' and sports reporters say 'the fastest bowler' — that's degrees of comparison.

items.text: This is the ___ day of my life!
My cold is ___ today than yesterday.
Of all the senses, sight seemed the ___ precious to her.

quiz.q: What is the comparative degree of 'good'?
quiz.explain: 'Good' is irregular: good – better – best.
quiz.mistake: Adds -er to an irregular adjective

quiz.q: What is the superlative degree of 'bad'?
quiz.explain: 'Bad' is irregular: bad – worse – worst.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the comparative 'worse' with the superlative 'worst'

quiz.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: Mount Everest is the most high mountain in the world.
Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.
Mount Everest is highest than all mountains.
Mount Everest is the higher mountain in the world.
quiz.explain: Comparing with all mountains needs the superlative with 'the': the highest.
quiz.mistake: Uses the comparative when comparing more than two

quiz.q: What is the comparative degree of 'happy'?
quiz.explain: When an adjective ends in consonant + y, change y to i and add -er: happier.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the y → i spelling rule or uses 'more' with -er

quiz.q: 'Of all my senses, I think sight is the ___ precious.'
quiz.explain: 'Of all' compares many, so we need the superlative 'most'.
quiz.mistake: Uses the comparative when comparing more than two

quiz.q: What is the comparative degree of 'big'?
quiz.explain: Short words ending in one vowel + one consonant double the last letter: big → bigger.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the final consonant

quiz.q: Which sentence is in the positive degree?
options: Ravi is the tallest in class.
quiz.explain: 'Tall' describes Ravi without comparing — positive degree.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any sentence with an adjective is comparative

quiz.q: 'In May, Delhi is ___ than Shimla.'
quiz.explain: Two places are compared with 'than', so the comparative 'hotter' is needed.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the word 'than'

teach.ask: Gappu says, 'This mango is gooder than that one, and it is the most best!' Help him with degrees of comparison.
teach.praise: Ah! This mango is better, and that one is the best! Yum!
teach.nudge: What are the correct words instead of 'gooder' and 'most best'?
